newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil uneasy as police strike turns violent.
newsitem.headline: Brazil uneasy as police strike turns violent.

text.p: The Brazilian government on Friday said it was becoming concerned about a month-long police strike that has spread across the country and this week erupted for a second time into violence.
"We are concerned and we are paying attention," Justice Minister Iris Rezende told reporters after talks with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

In the northeastern state of Alagoas, where the law of the gun runs wild and civil servants have not been paid in nine months, tensions came to a head on Thursday when striking police battled with troops outside the legislative assembly.

The gunfight, in which three police officers were injured, was reminiscent of a confrontation between striking civil police and military police last month in the city of Belo Horizonte, capital of the state of Minas Gerais. One person died.
The flare-up in Alagoas sent shock waves through Brazil and made the police officers' strike, largely ignored since the bloodshed in Belo Horizonte, headline material once more.
"Police threaten country," said Friday's Jornal do Brasil newspaper. "On strike, threatening governors, often with their pistols drawn, the police are creating a climate of instability."

The stoppages began in late June in Minas Gerais, where governor Eduardo Azeredo quickly caved in and awarded a 48.2 percent pay rise to the civil police, extra spending the state, strapped for cash like all others, could ill afford.
The strikes have since spread through 15 of Brazil's 27 states and the army has been called out to protect local government buildings in four states.
At the heart of the dispute lies money.
Brazilian police are notoriously poorly paid, often forced to supplement their income by working as bodyguards when off duty or, quite frequently, turning to crime and extortion.
In the northern state of Tocantins, the basic wage of a police recruit is about $330 a month.
"Tocantin wages are considered on the high side," said a Justice Ministry spokeswoman.

As for the states, which set and pay police wages, years of financial imprudence have left them virtually bankrupt and unable to pay extra. Most are renegotiating their huge debts with the federal government in return for mass layoffs.
Brasilia says the strikes are a concern of the states.

"There's no situation of crisis. The federal government has tried to give the states whatever help it can, that is, offering to make troops available to ensure order and security," said presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral late on Thursday.

In addition to Alagoas, troops are on the streets of Joao Pessoa, capital of the northeastern state of Paraiba, in Porto Allegre, capital of Rio Grande do Sul state, and in Recife, capital of Pernambuco state.
